title: 20 years as a software engineer, 2 months of free-time evenings (about 2 h a day) on my first game: a pixel roguelite made with Claude Code and PixelLab. Not vibe coding. Here's the workflow; how would you improve it?
author: strongwinderic
selftext:
I've been a software engineer for 20 years, and this is my first game: **Scraplings**, a pixel-art roguelite for Android (landscape, touch or controller). A small maintenance bot salvages a factory that never got the shutdown order. It's coming soon, and before launch I'd like this community's opinion.

It's a side project: I work on it in my free time, about two hours a day, for the last two months. So all of this is roughly 120 hours of my time, which is a big part of why I'm sharing the workflow.

**How I use AI (it isn't vibe coding)**

AI writes most of the code and makes everything faster. I take every creative decision: what the game is, what goes in, what gets cut, how it should feel. AI suggests; I accept it, push back or steer it. In practice:

* **A written plan before any code.** Each feature starts as a plan: the problem, the approach, what's out of scope, how it gets tested. Claude Code writes it, I change it until I agree, and only then does it build. 50+ plans so far.
* **A decision record for every call that could have gone either way:** 72 of them, from currencies to "melee stops at walls". When I change my mind, the record gets an update instead of a rewrite, so the AI always knows *why* things are the way they are.
* **CI that won't merge red.** Every change is a pull request that runs a headless smoke test (about 430 checks: it plays rooms, fights, walks every menu with a controller) and a localization guard (13 languages, no hardcoded text, nothing off screen). A beta is one button: GitHub Actions builds, signs and uploads it to Google Play's closed test.
* **I play every build and write notes,** and my notes become the next plan. Seven playtest rounds so far. After one of them I threw out auto-attack and had the combat rebuilt around aimed attack chains and a dash.
* **Art:** the robots, enemies and factory tiles were generated with PixelLab and cleaned up. The UI, icons, weapons and effects are pixel art drawn by Python scripts, where every pixel is a character in a text grid. Claude writes them, I review them, and they re-render any time I want a change.
* **Sound and music** are synthesized from code as well: a tiny chiptune tracker in Python.

**What I'd love your opinion on**

1. Does the clip show what the game is in its first few seconds?
2. Where do you draw the line between "AI-assisted" and "AI-made"? Would you describe mine differently?
3. How would you improve this workflow? I'm especially curious how others handle animation and effects: generate and clean up, or draw with code?

Happy to go deep on any of it: the plan format, the prompts, the CI. If you have an Android phone, there are closed-beta codes in the comments.

Claude helped me tidy this post's English; the opinions are mine.

Hey man , thanks for the code , ive got it and playing it , its pretty fun, the sprite jumping size and shape when spinning around is a bit jarring, the movement is smooth which is nice, the telegraph of attacks is good, would be nice to have some more meaty feeling in the swings for the forst weapon.

replies.author: strongwinderic

Thanks for playing and for the detail! Noted on the spin jump and the first weapon’s swings. A pass on how hits land goes out in the next beta, and I’m working on the sprite size jump. Would love to hear if it feels better.  
Feel free to use it as inspiration, and please share it with me when you have something to show :)

comments.author: chonky_totoro

replies.author: strongwinderic
replies.body:
Honestly, I feel that. My 20 years weren't the main thing that made this game happen. Doing it the old way, I don't think I'd have had the time: it's a side project, about two hours a day.

Knowing software, processes and code does help. It's how I keep the AI on a leash with plans, tests and CI. But what really made it possible was handing off the grunt work and spending my time on the creative decisions: what the game is, what goes in, what gets cut, how it should feel.

And you're right that the art is where it shows. The graphics and animations still need a lot of work. Maybe AI gets there in the next few years, or maybe the right call is to hire an artist to polish it. If the game earns it, I'd happily pay one.

In the end, I don't know how much longer I'll have a job as a traditional software engineer with where AI is going. So I'm betting on building my own products instead of waiting to find out.

comments.author: CodeGuyJay

What do you mean AI writes “most of the code”, just curious what code did you write?

I’m also a software engineer with a decade of experience, but I don’t touch any of the code. I find it’s easier not to worry about it altogether - I do all the steps you describe but I’d still describe it as vibe coding lol

replies.author: strongwinderic
replies.body: Fair question. I pick the framework, the patterns, the specs and the platforms, and Claude writes the code. I don’t read it line by line, but I review it day to day so the project doesn’t turn into a Frankenstein. By your definition that’s vibe coding, and I’m fine owning it.

comments.author: Beniskickbutt
comments.body:
Looks great, I feel you on the 20 years as a dev with only 2hrs a day..

AI is awesome. I've peridiocally poked around with making a game every once in a w hile but Im a professional senior dev that works 9 hrs\~ a day.  My time with family has always been too valuable to give up.

AI has helped me focus on the design and bring ideas to life while not needing to type out each and every little detail. Can throw a design pattern at it and its good to go. Now I get to develop and keep the time with the family. When you need to you can go into the nitty gritty.

comments.author: strongwinderic
comments.body: Yep, vibe coding with guardrails. I think the term got a bad name because of slop: a vague prompt, no review, accept everything. Specs, plans, tests and review are the opposite of that, so I’d rather reclaim the word than dodge it.
